title: Exclusion Audits: Where Demands Exceed Capability
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Exclusion Audits: Where Demands Exceed Capability.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An exclusion audit makes the interaction between design demand and available capability visible across an end-to-end outcome. It examines sensory, motor, cognitive, linguistic, technical, financial, temporal, geographic, and social demands, plus the consequence of mismatch.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Audit exclusion as a chain of demands
turns.text: What changes when we look at audit exclusion as a chain of demands?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not add estimated exclusion percentages mechanically across steps; the same people may encounter several barriers and conditions interact. Quantitative estimates can compare options or show scale when population and capability data are appropriate, but they cannot replace lived evidence or represent every intersection.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use three levels:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: component: can a control be perceived and operated? journey: can a person preserve understanding and progress across states, channels, and time? service system: can policy, staff, vendors, physical access, and support fulfil an equivalent outcome?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: At each level record not only inability, but extra effort, dependence, privacy loss, uncertainty, cost, and delayed recovery. “Completed with daughter’s help” is not independent success if the person did not choose that assistance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build an exclusion register?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Trace preparation, entry, authentication, primary task, waiting, fulfilment, exception, support, and recovery. For each demand record:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: legitimate purpose and whether it is necessary; conditions that intensify it; affected people and intersections; evidence and confidence; workaround, helper, and transferred burden; severity, duration, and reversibility of consequence; remove, reduce, support, alternative, or policy response; owner, dependency, due point, and verification; residual exclusion after action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prioritise through consequence, reach, recurrence, equity, and structural leverage. A component repair can remove barriers across many journeys; a policy change can remove the need for an inaccessible interaction entirely. Do not let implementation effort determine whether a right or essential service is provided.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Validate alternative-route equivalence across availability, time, money, privacy, dignity, information, decision authority, and final outcome. A staffed phone line available two hours per week is not equivalent to a continuous digital route.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: public-benefit application?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A claimant may individually manage identity proof, a long form, evidence upload, and deadline. Combined with low bandwidth, variable work, unfamiliar legal language, and fear of error, the journey becomes impossible. Reducing each screen’s friction is inadequate if policy still requires unavailable documents or support cannot decide exceptions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Screen-bound audit: physical, human, policy, and vendor barriers disappear. Barrier arithmetic: overlapping estimates become false population precision. Completion-only evidence: coerced help and privacy loss count as success. Bottleneck migration: one demand falls while the next becomes dominant. Inferior fallback: the alternative has less authority, inventory, or quality.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Heat-map theatre: coloured cells replace owner, action, and verification.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Convert mismatch into an owned intervention
turns.text: What changes when we look at convert mismatch into an owned intervention?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The audit uses representative states rather than a perfect screen. Clinic comparison includes long content, unknown access data, map alternatives, zoom, keyboard, screen reader, and interruption. Transfer includes consequence, session expiry, network uncertainty, and assisted completion.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Each mismatch records affected conditions, consequence, existing workaround, evidence, severity, owner, dependency, and verification.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interventions can remove demand, provide an equivalent route, support adaptation, change policy or data, preserve state, add human assistance, or redesign the service. The team avoids mechanically counting estimated exclusion across steps because the same people face several barriers and conditions interact.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Priority follows access to the core outcome and consequence, not the easiest conformance fix.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The audit remains connected to production. Findings become acceptance criteria, design-system changes, service interventions, and monitoring. Temporary exceptions have mitigation and expiry. Disabled people help interpret and evaluate the system without being asked to represent everyone or repeatedly prove the same known barrier.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: identity verification?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Requiring a sharp photo, precise head movement, recent document, private room, and stable connection creates interacting demands. An exclusion audit can lead to alternative evidence, assisted verification, resumable flow, and accountable review rather than a more encouraging camera animation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners use exclusion audits to change roadmaps, contracts, service levels, and outcome definitions. They preserve critical cases even when population evidence is incomplete and publish residual exclusions honestly. The audit is repeated after change because capability, technology, policy, and the service ecosystem evolve.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Audit the mismatch at every step
turns.text: What changes when we look at audit the mismatch at every step?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The audit links every mismatch to evidence, affected conditions, existing alternative, severity, owner, and verification method. Teams prioritise by exclusion and consequence, not ease of fixing. The resulting backlog includes component repair, content change, alternative route, data improvement, service policy, and research at the edge.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a passport-renewal service. An audit follows the complete task and compares demands—reading, memory, fine motor control, document access, time, and travel—with varied capabilities and situations. A route may technically pass a screen-level accessibility check while still excluding someone who cannot obtain or upload the required file.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Follow a service beyond its digital “success” screen. What document, call, journey, payment, or human approval is still required? Identify who can complete the interface yet remain excluded from the outcome.
